documents.title: Analytical Platform Architecture Intent
documents.description: Architecture intent for fedc's analytical platform modernisation, establishing the chosen direction for self-service analytics in response to ADR-013.
documents.scope: Self-Service Analytics initiative — the analytical platform layer covering ingestion, storage, transformation, and consumption of enterprise data. Directly aligned to ADR-013.

executive-summary.summary: This intent sets fedc's direction for analytical platform modernisation: a Databricks lakehouse as the enterprise data tier, with Oracle Analytics Cloud retained as the self-service BI layer.
points: Chosen over a full SaaS replacement (too costly and high-risk) and a native-OAC-only approach (no ML tier, cannot meet latency).
Event-driven ingestion from CC&B, MDM, and ERP via the Confluent event broker meets sub-15-minute latency targets.
Preserves existing OAC investment while adding an ML-ready tier governed by Unity Catalog.

documents.intent-statement: fedc will adopt a lakehouse architecture on Databricks as its enterprise data platform, with Oracle Analytics Cloud (OAC) retained as the self-service consumption layer. Data will be ingested from Oracle CC&B, MDM, and ERP via event-driven pipelines through the Confluent event broker. This approach avoids replacing OAC (preserving existing user investment and training), while providing a modern, scalable storage and transformation tier that can serve both BI and ML workloads.
documents.background: fedc's current analytical landscape is fragmented: operational reports are generated directly from Oracle CC&B via custom OBIEE dashboards, commercial teams extract data to Excel for modelling, and there is no governed enterprise data store. The Oracle Analytics Cloud (OAC) licence is underutilised — it is connected only to CC&B and lacks a governed semantic layer. ADR-013 has been raised to address this fragmentation. The architecture intent decision centres on how to modernise the platform: whether to invest in OAC natively, adopt a fully cloud-native SaaS alternative, or introduce a lakehouse tier beneath OAC.

drivers.description: Business demand for self-service analytics is increasing — operational managers require real-time views of metering, payment, and grid data without IT-mediated report production.
Ofgem half-hourly settlement mandates require sub-30-minute data latency for settlement-related datasets by 2027.
AI/ML workloads for churn prediction and predictive asset maintenance require a scalable, ML-ready data tier that CC&B cannot provide directly.

options-considered.name: Cloud-Native SaaS (e.g. Snowflake + Tableau)
options-considered.description: Replace the existing Oracle analytics stack with a cloud-native SaaS data warehouse (Snowflake) and a best-of-breed BI tool (Tableau or Power BI), migrating all existing OAC content.
pros: Best-in-class SaaS scalability and managed infrastructure
Strong ecosystem for ML integration via Snowpark
Widely adopted in UK utilities sector
cons: High migration cost and risk — all existing OAC content and training is stranded
Oracle ERP and CC&B integration complexity on non-Oracle platforms
Additional licensing cost on top of existing Oracle contracts
18–24 month migration timeline before operational benefit

options-considered.name: Extend Oracle Analytics Cloud natively
options-considered.description: Invest in OAC's native data integration (Oracle Data Integrator) and semantic layer capabilities, connecting OAC directly to CC&B, MDM, and ERP without introducing a separate lakehouse tier.
pros: Fully within existing Oracle contractual and support boundary
No new tooling — builds on existing OAC skills
Faster initial delivery for incremental BI use cases
cons: Oracle Data Integrator is not suited for real-time event-driven ingestion at scale
No native ML-ready data tier — Sagemaker and Databricks integration is complex
Limited support for open data formats (Delta Lake, Parquet) needed for ML feature stores
Perpetuates tight coupling to Oracle CC&B as the analytical source

options-considered.name: Lakehouse on Databricks with OAC as BI layer
options-considered.description: Introduce Databricks as the enterprise data lakehouse (Delta Lake, Unity Catalog for governance), feeding OAC via a semantic layer (OAC Data Gateway or direct Databricks SQL connector). Event-driven ingestion via Confluent.
pros: Decouples BI consumption from source systems — OAC connects to governed lakehouse, not raw CC&B
Databricks supports both BI (SQL) and ML (Python/Spark) workloads on the same platform
Unity Catalog provides fine-grained governance and lineage required for UK GDPR and Ofgem audit
Preserves OAC investment — existing content and user skills are retained
Event-driven ingestion via Confluent achieves sub-15-minute latency targets
cons: Introduces new tooling (Databricks) requiring upskilling of Data Engineering team
OAC-to-Databricks connector is via JDBC — not natively certified by Oracle

documents.recommended-direction: Option 3 — Lakehouse on Databricks with OAC as BI layer — is the recommended direction. It is the only option that simultaneously achieves sub-15-minute data latency, preserves existing OAC investment, and provides an ML-ready data tier for future AI workloads. The JDBC connector risk is mitigated by Oracle's published OAC-Databricks integration guidance and fedc's existing AWS infrastructure. Option 1 is deferred for strategic review post-2027 pending Oracle contract renewal. Option 2 is rejected due to its inability to support ML workloads and real-time latency requirements.

open-questions.question: Can Oracle Support confirm that the OAC-to-Databricks SQL connector is within the standard OAC support boundary, or will fedc require a separate support agreement with Databricks for this integration path?
What is the agreed Databricks workspace tiering model — will operational and commercial teams share a single workspace with Unity Catalog namespace separation, or require separate workspaces?

documents.title: Integration Platform Architecture Intent
documents.description: Architecture intent for the modernisation of fedc's integration landscape, establishing the role of the Confluent event broker and Oracle Integration Cloud within the target integration architecture.
documents.scope: Integration landscape modernisation — covering the iPaaS layer, point-to-point integrations between CC&B, CRM, ERP, MDM, and the lakehouse, and the adoption of event-driven patterns across fedc's application estate.

executive-summary.summary: This intent establishes a hybrid integration architecture: Confluent Kafka as the enterprise event backbone for real-time flows and Oracle Integration Cloud for synchronous API orchestration.
points: All new integrations must route through this iPaaS tier; bespoke middleware and direct database links are decommissioned on a schedule.
Chosen over a single managed iPaaS (cost-prohibitive at scale) and retaining ODI batch (cannot meet latency or lineage needs).
Maximises existing Oracle investment and provides Ofgem-ready audit trails and data lineage.

documents.intent-statement: fedc will adopt a hybrid integration architecture combining Confluent Kafka as the enterprise event backbone for real-time, high-volume data flows and Oracle Integration Cloud (OIC) as the API management and orchestration layer for synchronous service integrations. All new integrations must be routed via this iPaaS tier; direct application-to-application database links and bespoke middleware will be decommissioned on a scheduled basis.
documents.background: fedc's current integration landscape has grown organically and includes a mix of Oracle Data Integrator batch jobs, direct database links between CC&B and MDM, and several bespoke Java middleware components connecting Salesforce to CC&B. This creates a fragile, hard-to-govern integration mesh with no central observability. The integration platform modernisation intent is being driven by the Data & Analytics Programme (which requires event streams from CC&B) and the CX Transformation Programme (which requires real-time CRM-to-CIS sync).

drivers.description: Multiple concurrent programmes (Data & Analytics, CX Transformation, Smart Meter Rollout) each require real-time data flows that the existing batch-based integration layer cannot deliver.
Bespoke Java middleware components connecting Salesforce and CC&B are reaching end-of-support and are not maintainable by the current team.
Ofgem requires auditable, time-stamped data lineage for settlement-related data flows — the current batch ODI approach cannot provide this without significant manual effort.

options-considered.name: Fully managed iPaaS (e.g. MuleSoft Anypoint)
options-considered.description: Replace all existing integration with a single MuleSoft Anypoint platform providing both event streaming (via Anypoint MQ) and API management.
pros: Single vendor, single platform for all integration patterns
Strong governance, monitoring, and API catalogue out-of-box
cons: High licensing cost — Anypoint pricing at fedc's integration volume is significantly above Confluent + OIC
MuleSoft's Kafka-compatible event streaming does not match Confluent's throughput and ecosystem maturity
Displaces existing Oracle Integration Cloud investment

options-considered.name: Retain ODI batch + extend with point-to-point APIs
options-considered.description: Continue with Oracle Data Integrator for batch data flows and add REST APIs on a case-by-case basis for real-time needs, without adopting a central event backbone.
cons: Cannot meet sub-15-minute latency requirements for analytics or CRM sync
Proliferates point-to-point complexity — no central observability
Does not address Ofgem lineage requirements

options-considered.name: Confluent event backbone + Oracle Integration Cloud (OIC)
options-considered.description: Confluent Kafka as the enterprise event backbone for all high-volume, real-time data streams; OIC for synchronous API orchestration and transformation. All new integrations must use one of these two patterns.
pros: Confluent provides enterprise Kafka with Schema Registry, governed connectors, and Ofgem-ready audit trails
OIC is already licensed and familiar to the integration team for synchronous patterns
Separation of concerns: event-driven (Confluent) vs request-reply (OIC) is well-understood
Kafka Connect provides certified connectors for CC&B, Salesforce, and Databricks
cons: Requires upskilling on Kafka administration and Schema Registry governance
Two platforms to operate and monitor — tooling integration (observability) requires investment

documents.recommended-direction: Option 3 — Confluent event backbone combined with Oracle Integration Cloud — is the recommended direction. It maximises existing Oracle investment, meets latency and lineage requirements, and provides a clear separation between event-driven and synchronous integration patterns. Option 1 is cost-prohibitive at fedc's scale. Option 2 cannot meet programme requirements and is rejected.

open-questions.question: What is the target decommission date for the existing bespoke Java middleware connecting Salesforce and CC&B? This is on the critical path for the CX Transformation Programme.
Should Oracle Data Integrator (ODI) be retained for any ongoing batch ETL use cases (e.g. ERP period-end extracts), or is OIC capable of replacing all ODI patterns within the programme scope?
